item.title: Trump won't reimburse taxpayers for TV ads after changing how they're funded
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump said Monday night that he will no longer use taxpayer funds to pay for a multimillion-dollar pro-Trump ad blitz ahead of the midterm elections, saying his super PAC will now pay for them. But he appears to have no plans to reimburse the federal government for funds already used on the ads, a White House official said Tuesday. “The President’s [social media post] was not referring to reimbursement," the official told ABC News. While Trump dismissed criticism of the ads as "a rather standard thing to do," he posted Monday that he had decided to pay for them on his own dime. "I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc," Trump wrote, referring to his super PAC. Eric Lee/Reuters - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks with media before boarding Marine One as he travels to Grand Island, Nebraska, on the South Lawn of the White House, Oct. 5, 2026. The move came after the U.S. government bankrolled a series of ads that aired nationally and heavily featured the president. One of the ads was a direct copy of a spot Trump's campaign ran in 2024. A White House official confirmed to ABC News Monday night that MAGA Inc. will pay for ads moving forward but defended them as something previous administrations have used. "Presidential Public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction," the official said. Trump defends spending millions on taxpayer-funded promotional ads: 'For the country' Earlier Monday, Vice President JD Vance defended using taxpayer money to run the ads, claiming they are "public service announcements." "They're not partisan. They're not -- you know, it's not like we're advocating for a particular candidate. We're trying to tell a story, I think, about how great the United States of America is," Vance said. Trump defended the ads last week at an event in the Oval Office, saying they were "for the spirit of our country" and not a political endorsement for Republican candidates on the ballot this November or for his administration's policies. "You have to understand; I'm not promoting a candidate. I'm not promoting myself because I'm not running for office. I'm promoting the country," Trump said. "Now, if somebody said that that's wrong, I'll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country," he said. U.S. Government - PHOTO: A fourth taxpayer-funded ad that promotes President Donald Trump’s policies ahead of the midterm elections shows scenes of Trump and the U.S. military amid the war in Iran as audio of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the president play over them. Trump has implored Republican voters to "pretend" that he is on the ballot in the November midterm elections to boost voter turnout for GOP congressional candidates. The federal government has spent at least $2.5 million to air the TV ads, according to an estimate from AdImpact, an advertising agency that analyzes ad spending across television. A total of $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security's budget had been allocated for the effort. Ethics watchdogs and several Congressional Democrats -- as well as some Republicans -- have said the ads are inappropriate. Some critics have said the ads could violate federal propaganda law. Four ads have been aired over the last two weeks. One features Trump in monochrome, slowly walking down a hallway, describing "the final battle" against "the deep state," "the globalists," and "the sick political class that hates our country." U.S. government video - PHOTO: The Trump administration appeared to run an ad on Fox News that has drawn criticism from Democrats as violating federal rules preventing the use of tax dollars for political purposes. Another ad includes a montage of clips and images of Trump at events and rallies featuring onscreen text about the "largest tax cuts in history." The latest ad, released last week, focuses on the U.S. war with Iran, now in its eighth month. Audio of Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plays in the background as U.S. military footage, including unclassified strikes, is displayed. The video in the ad appears to be the same as one played during the Republican midterm convention last month. And it played last Wednesday before Hegseth addressed 600 service members in his State of the Force speech at the Marine Corps base at Quantico, Virginia. item.title: Trump allies push to sideline AI safety advocates as fight over oversight grows
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
BERKELEY, Calif. - After artificial intelligence safety advocates captured Washington’s attention with dire warnings about the technology’s power, the Trump administration and its allies embraced some of their suggestions, while moving to sideline the advocates themselves. Battle lines have been drawn in recent days over part of an accord signed by President Donald Trump and AI chief executives last week: Who should audit AI companies’ systems to ensure their technology behaves as intended. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Leading AI companies - including OpenAI and Anthropic - have for years worked with a cluster of nonprofits concentrated in the Bay Area’s AI safety community, which grew out of the effective altruism movement. But Trump’s tech-world allies say the work of auditing AI should be taken on by America’s largest consulting firms. “In my view they should be professional auditors, not these NGOs,” investor and former top White House AI adviser David Sacks said on his All-In podcast last week. He said in a post on X last month that the AI safety nonprofit METR, which has worked with Anthropic, was too close to the company to be called independent. Soon after, Anthropic said it would partner with consulting giant Accenture to build a team of outside evaluators. At a conference here over the weekend, members of AI safety organizations grappled with the impact of what some see as a coordinated campaign to delegitimize their work and paint their community as cultish and unserious. The event took place at a former hotel popular with AI safety acolytes that also recently hosted a conference on AI consciousness and a sex workshop called “Slutcon.” Trump officials and allies have sniped at the movement for months but the attacks intensified after public anxiety over AI risks forced the White House to respond. Sacks last month shared on X a New York Post front page that called employees of METR, which helped OpenAI investigate its rogue AI agents, “THE WOKE WIZARDS OF AI.” (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.) Trump on Sunday named several figures who have rejected calls from advocates for an AI industry-wide slowdown to his Super Intelligence Force advisory panel. They include Sacks and Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, who said last month that calls for action to prevent extreme scenarios of AI causing harm promoted “extinction, death-cult-like philosophies.” “There has absolutely been a rhetorical push within certain corners of the White House and broader Trump administration to get the message out about effective altruism and its potential dangers,” said a Trump administration official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe private discussions. A White House official said that it supports organizations that evaluate the security and safety of how AI models are engineered. The official pointed to Trump’s 2025 executive order targeting what the president termed “woke AI.” Anthropic declined to comment. Nathan Leamer, director of the pro-industry nonprofit Build American AI, said he has been briefing congressional staff and other influential conservative figures in Washington about effective altruism, describing it as antithetical to his own Christian values. “A year ago no one in Hill offices knew what effective altruism was,” Leamer said. Build American AI is linked to Leading the Future, a political campaign group funded by the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, a major midterms Republican donor. Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, which says it is focused on AI policy in the public interest, said that Trump allies are trying discredit anyone pushing for meaningful AI regulation, an idea that now has significant momentum. “In D.C., at least, and maybe in the broader culture, we won that fight. The vibe is with us,” said Carson, who also leads a political advocacy organization funded in part by Anthropic. “People are very concerned. Congress wants to regulate.” But leaders of AI evaluation start-ups that did not grow out of the AI safety movement said some Washington Republicans are distrustful of the label. “It almost felt like a new version of McCarthyism,” said Rayan Krishnan, CEO of the Andreessen Horowitz-backed start-up Vals AI, after a trip to Washington last month to pitch his start-up to the public sector. Judd Rosenblatt, CEO of AE Studio, who described himself as a conservative small business owner, said multiple people in the Trump administration have told his team that they see the need for third parties to assess AI tools, but are wary of effective altruism, he said. Civil society groups that have been auditing AI systems since before the debut of ChatGPT warn there is a risk that an opportunity for oversight of opaque AI giants will be squandered. “Where we find ourselves now is trying to determine who will actually be in the room in making decisions,” said Miranda Bogen, chief technologist at the Center for Democracy & Technology and director of the advocacy group’s AI Governance Lab, one of various groups eager to contribute their expertise in standard-setting. The accord signed by AI chief executives last week, which Trump called “morally binding,” was frequently mentioned onstage and in huddles between sessions at the Berkeley conference last weekend, where attendees endured a heat wave with fans and Popsicles. At a Sunday discussion panel on what the AI auditor ecosystem might look like, one speaker said they are working on building a broad coalition of experts, including people working on bias and discrimination as well as blue-chip firms like Accenture and Deloitte. Panelists also discussed other ways the community could prove its legitimacy. Another suggested two-month boot camps to train a talent pipeline of qualified auditors. Adam Gleave, CEO of FAR.AI, a nonprofit research institute, said in an interview that excluding the AI safety community would shut out people with expertise that are important in the current moment. “When it comes to looking at millions of agent transcripts and trying to piece together what they did and how they were interacting, I don’t think there are many organizations in the world that have that expertise,” Gleave said. “The reality is that anyone you hire with that background is going to have some connection to the industry.” On his podcast, Sacks and his co-hosts, who remain close to the White House, made clear that they preferred instead to have established corporate giants do the work. “You’re going to see EY in short order here announce something,” said investor Chamath Palihapitiya, who earlier in the episode said his start-up 8090 was building the global accounting firm formerly known as Ernst & Young “an entire audit infrastructure for super intelligence,” and that 8090 now plans to “roll it out to everybody.” EY said in a statement that it was working with 8090 to “develop new capabilities that bring greater visibility, traceability and human accountability to consequential AI-enabled decisions and workflows.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/told-world-ai-dangerous-now-092510605.html

item.title: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declares state of emergency over spike in measles cases
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency on Monday as neighboring Pennsylvania battles its largest measles outbreak in three decades. As of Oct. 3, New York has recorded 108 measles cases so far this year, 92 of those since mid-July across 18 rural counties where communities are under-immunized, according to Hochul's order. "After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York State, I am declaring a state disaster emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease," Hochul said in a statement . "No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease." Measles cases surpass 1,000 in Pennsylvania amid the state's largest outbreak in decades It marks the first time a state has issued an emergency order since measles cases began rising last year. At least 95% of measles cases in the U.S. have been among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown. The order allows registered nurses to order the collection and testing of specimens for suspected measles cases. Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo - PHOTO: New York Governor Kathy Hochul speaks during a news conference, Oct. 2, 2026, in New York. Early symptoms include cough, runny nose, fever as high as 104 Fahrenheit and red, watery eyes, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Two to three days after symptoms start, patients may develop Koplik spots, which are tiny white spots that may appear inside the mouth on the inner cheek. Three to five days after symptoms start, patients may experience a rash, first appearing on the face at the hairline before moving downwards to the neck, chest, stomach, arms, legs and feet. Fever may spike even higher than 104 F when the rash appears, the CDC says. The order, in effect until Nov. 4, allows pharmacists in New York to vaccinate ⁠children as young as age 2 with the MMR shot. It also expands who can administer MMR vaccines to include emergency medical technicians-paramedics, advanced EMS and midwives. Additionally, it suspends a previous requirement that health care professionals who administer vaccines to those aged 19 and older receive consent before reporting vaccination to New York City or New York State immunizations registries. All MMR vaccinations of children and adults must be reported within 72 hours. How hospitals, clinics in Pennsylvania are responding to the measles outbreak "Department staff are working closely with local health departments and regional partners to track and contain the current measles outbreak," Dr. James McDonald, commissioner for the New York State Department, said in a statement. "The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is the best protection -- protecting nearly all people against disease who receive the recommended doses." The state said it has administered more than 1,000 MMR shots in rural areas since July. Meanwhile, Pennsylvania health officials are now reporting more than 1,000 measles cases. Nearly 200 people have been hospitalized and the state has reported five measles-associated deaths, which is the most any state has reported in over 30 years. This outbreak follows a trend of growing outbreaks in the U.S. over the last two years. Earlier this year, South Carolina reported the end to a measles outbreak of 997 cases. Last year, Texas reported an outbreak of 762 cases. Kateryna Kon/science Photo Library/Getty Images - PHOTO: Measles virus particle, illustration. Nationally, nearly 4,000 cases have been confirmed this year in the U.S., with infections reported in almost every state, according to the CDC . It's the highest number of illnesses from measles since 1991. The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective in preventing measles infection, and two doses are 97% effective, the CDC says. Infants aged 6 to 11 months living in or traveling to high-risk outbreak areas may receive an early third dose of the MMR vaccine. However, CDC data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2025-26 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 95.2% seen in the 2019-20 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. School vaccine exemptions also reached a record high last school year. Recent CDC data showed that vaccine exemptions for kindergarteners increased to 4.2% during the 2025-26 school year. This is up from 3.6% compared to the previous school year and 2.2% during the 2020-21 school year. item.title: Civilian cargo ship sinks and crew is missing after Black Sea drone attack
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Two injured crew members from one of the ships have been sent for treatment [Petko Momchilov / Reuters] A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say. A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued. Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine. Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable". Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said. The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania. It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board. A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched. Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain. Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan. Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law". He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable." He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning. "Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning." "Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable." Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea. [BBC] A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media. On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. item.title: S&P 500 hits record high as Nvidia nears $6 trillion milestone
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading last month in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago / Getty) The S&P 500 on Tuesday hit a record, as the index rose for a fourth straight day, supported by rising technology stocks, hopes for a positive earnings season, and a pause in oil’s recent surge. The broad-based closed higher by 0.58%, its first record closing high since Aug. 13. The Nasdaq Composite also jumped 0.45%. It also hit a record high for the second time this week. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq’s gains were overwhelmingly powered by gains in tech companies, such as chipmakers Marvell and Broadcom. Nvidia, the world’s largest public company, also rose and moved closer to becoming the first company to ever reach $6 trillion in market value. Other trillion-dollar tech stocks also rose Tuesday. Microsoft, Amazon, SpaceX, Meta Platforms and Tesla shares all traded in the green. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers the keynote address at the GTC AI Conference in San Jose, Calif., last year. (Josh Edelson / AFP via Getty) Investors are also looking forward to the start of the third quarter’s earnings season, which begins in earnest next week with the country’s biggest banks reporting their results. “Heading into the start of the earnings season, analysts and companies have been more optimistic than normal in their earnings outlooks for the third quarter,” said FactSet senior earnings analyst John Butters. Artificial intelligence stocks are set to be a major contributor. “At the stock level, AI infrastructure stocks are expected to drive more than half of S&P 500 EPS growth in Q3,” said analysts at Goldman Sachs on Friday. They forecast that Nvidia and chipmaker Micron would likely be responsible for a third of the entire S&P 500’s earnings growth this quarter. Oil static Stocks got off to a strong start Tuesday thanks to a drop in oil prices. However, by the end of the trading day, energy prices were about flat. That did little to deter the rally in stocks, though. Brent oil futures ended the day up 0.2% at $100.58 per barrel, but that came after an earlier drop of as much as 3.3%. U.S. crude oil ended the day up just one cent at $89.44 per barrel. Earlier, it was down more than 2.8%. Oil’s muted session after a report from Bloomberg News said that Saudi Arabia’s key cross-country pipeline was operating normally, after “multiple attacks” took the critical pipeline out of commission in early September. Saudi Aramco has not responded to multiple requests for comment from NBC News. Three-phase spheroids stand behind pipelines at Saudi Aramco's crude oil processing facility, in Abqaiq, Saudi Arabia, in 2019. (Dina Khrennikova / Bloomberg via Getty) The pipeline has been used as a Strait of Hormuz workaround, given that shipping traffic there remains at just a fraction of pre-Iran war levels. Still, “the market remains nervous about potential supply disruptions from the region,” said ING commodities analysts overnight. “This nervousness is likely to persist until there are signs of progress in a deal between the US and Iran. In the meantime, the risk of further escalation remains very real.” Bond watch Treasury yields also declined slightly, after hitting fresh 24-year highs on Monday. The 10-year yield was still at more than 5.27%. The 30-year Treasury was about flat at 5.6%. While the yield, or the rate, on both of those bonds have been at their highest levels since 2002, some experts think they’re close to topping out. “Several forces suggest rates may peak within the next month,” said Apollo’s Torsten Slok on Tuesday. “Approaching midterm elections raise the odds of a Middle East deal that would lower oil prices,” he added. President Donald Trump has said multiple times recently that he he believes a deal could be reached with Iran to end the 7-month war “right after” the midterm elections are over. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said Sept. 9. Those comments marked a turn after Trump for months said that the war would last only a short period of time. “A deal or government action that lowers oil prices would ease the upward pressure on interest rates at a time when yields are already elevated across nearly the entire global bond market,” Slok added. item.title: Police and students clash in France as high school unrest intensifies
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The interior ministry said 86,000 had joined the protests, unions gave a higher figure (ROMEO BOETZLE) Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday, as unions and teachers joined high school students who for days have been demanding better learning conditions in protests punctuated by violent confrontations. Students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds since late September, complaining of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures. Unions, rights groups and the children have accused the authorities of using disproportionate force -- a police stun grenade tore the hand off one teenager on Monday and another youngster had his teeth knocked out last week after police fired a grenade launcher at his head. At the Place de la Republique in central Paris, the savoury smell of grilled merguez sausages -- a French protest staple -- wafted over the crowd. Two men in climbing gear scaled the nearby monument, where they unfurled a plastic banner reading "Neglected schools, sacrificed youth". "Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard," 19-year-old Lilia told AFP at a massive march in central Paris, adding she hoped the president would listen. The unrest has erupted with just months to go before the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with far-right veteran candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction. "I'm afraid for my future," Selma, 15, told AFP without giving her surname, among the thousands marching in the country's second largest city of Marseille. The interior ministry said 86,000 had already joined demonstrations across the rest of the country earlier Tuesday. The CGT union put the figure at 260,000 people. - 'At war' - Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu responded to the demonstrations, telling lawmakers in the National Assembly that there was "no room for tolerance of violence". "Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings," he told parliament, adding it was a "lie" to suggest the government had ordered "police repression" against protesters. While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police. Police have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds. The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement. A 15-year-old lost a hand to a sting-ball grenade fired by riot officers in the northern town of Lens on Monday. The prosecutor's office in the northeastern town of Metz meanwhile said he called for a police inquiry over a possible sexual assault on a minor younger than 15, after video footage circulated of what appeared to be a plainclothes policeman groping a female pupil he had detained. The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of being behind the movement. Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods. - Thousands of arrests - Thomas, a 17-year-old student from the Paris suburb of Val-de-Marne, said some of the classrooms at his school were short of desks and chairs while the bathrooms lacked doors, toilet paper and soap. "We just want better conditions for studying," he told AFP. Adults turned out in droves Tuesday to support the young demonstrators. Standing outside a school in Rennes, in western France, teacher Romain Dubourg told AFP he and colleagues had "talked about the police brutality we've witnessed" and decided to show up for the pupils. In the eastern city of Lyon, Sandrine Buteau was among dozens of parents who organised to support the youngsters. "As adults, we're a bit like the security cordon," she said. Lyon teacher Rindala Younes said she was present to help the students "convey their message peacefully". "The high school students' demands are legitimate," she said. Amnesty International late Monday said the French authorities should "put an end to the disproportionate police repression seen in recent days during student protests". The police have launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late Monday. Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education ministry. More than 5,000 people, 87 percent of them minors, have been arrested. item.title: Trump administration unveils plan to tie high birth and marriage rates to transit funding
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Communities with high birth and marriage rates could soon gain an advantage in securing federal transit money — a long-sought goal of the Trump administration but one that a top Democratic appropriator calls "bizarre and dystopian." The Federal Transit Administration wants to revamp a multibillion-dollar program that helps state and local authorities fund infrastructure projects such as rail improvements and new bus lanes. Public feedback on the administration's plan, which was rolled out Oct. 1, is being accepted through mid-November. The idea would fulfill a priority of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to steer grant money to parts of the country with birth and marriage rates higher than the national average, a policy initiative he unveiled shortly after being sworn into office early last year . Under the transit proposal , the FTA would cover up to 10 percentage points more of a project's costs if an area's average birth and marriage rates meet, exceed or are just below nationwide thresholds. "Moving forward, the federal government is focusing on smart, affordable projects with high ridership. If you want federal funding, your project needs to align with where communities and families are actually growing," the Transportation Department said in a statement. But the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee had harsh words for the proposal. "Tying funding for transit projects to marriage rates and how many babies a woman has is the sort of bizarre and dystopian idea you'd expect in a TV show, not actual policy put forth by the U.S. government — yet here we are," Sen. Patty Murray of Washington state said in a statement. She said President Donald Trump "wants to weaponize federal grants to wage his backward culture wars and punish Democrats." Spokespeople for Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), ranking member of the House Appropriations Committee, didn't respond to a request for comment. A former FTA administrator during the Obama administration also was critical. "It's throwing a bone to these ideologues who want to incentivize child rearing and marriage," said Peter Rogoff, who previously led Sound Transit in the Seattle area and is now a transportation consultant. "But it's ludicrous on its face to try to achieve that goal through an infrastructure program. "Does anyone really believe that there are couples out there saying, 'Hey, sweetheart, you and I should get married and raise a passel of kids because a dozen years from now, maybe they'll build light rail out to our neighborhood?'" he asked. Duffy, who has nine children, has urged young people to tie the knot and " have lots of kids ." He's one of several Cabinet members with big families, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, DHS head Markwayne Mullin and Health and Human Services chief Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The national fertility rate sank to a record low in 2025 — 53.1 births per 1,000 women ages 15 to 44. Trump has said he will be known as the "fertilization president." The FTA grant program hinges on a lengthy approval process that can take years for applicants to navigate, with money becoming available after a binding grant agreement is executed. Before reaching the final step, the FTA determines how much of a project's total cost it will cover. The share of federal funding is capped at 60 percent for new, large transit infrastructure and 80 percent for boosting the capacity of existing systems. For those two types of projects, the administration now wants to calculate the amount it will fund using a formula that, in part, would be based on a transit corridor's average birth and marriage rates. When those rates are at or above national benchmarks, or just below them, the federal share would be increased — rising by up to 10 percentage points. Under Duffy, DOT has launched a "Make Travel Family Friendly Again" campaign, encouraging airports to create play areas and add nursing rooms at terminals. He also has sought to inspire families to travel around the country via his "The Great American Road Trip" video series . The birth and marriage rates proposal has yet to be finalized, and it's unknown when it will be. It also wasn't immediately clear which exact communities would benefit from the idea. The plan is part of a wider effort by the FTA to rewrite its guidance for federal Capital Investment Grants, or CIG. The public can weigh in through Nov. 16. CIG and a related pilot initiative got $1.7 billion from Congress for fiscal 2026 on top of $1.6 billion in additional funding from the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law. Projects that previously won money from the program include the ongoing construction of the Gateway rail tunnel between New York and New Jersey and a pending extension of Chicago's Red Line train . Paul Skoutelas, CEO and president of the American Public Transportation Association, said in a statement the organization is reviewing the FTA plan. Rogoff, the former FTA administrator, said the framework would "clearly disadvantage" projects in areas with lower birth and marriage rates, adding that federal law doesn't require that this data be relied on when carrying out CIG. "Obviously, the program is about moving people — not about moving married people or moving parents," he said. item.title: Former Army major who killed 13 in Fort Hood shooting to be executed by firing squad
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad, the Pentagon announced Monday. "Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell wrote on X . He added, "The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come." The U.S. military has not carried out an execution since 1961 and has not used a firing squad to execute a service member since World War II. The announcement of Trump's approval came days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection. The failed execution prompted Tennessee's governor to halt further executions this year and order a third-party review. Asked whether the failed execution in Tennessee would lead him to seek changes to capital punishment, Trump called it "an interesting situation." He told reporters in Denton, Texas, that carrying out lethal injections "shouldn't be very difficult." Trump's approval sets in motion a series of procedural steps toward carrying out Hasan's execution. But Hasan could put the process on hold — potentially for years — by filing a habeas corpus appeal challenging the legality of his detention in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer. Hasan was convicted in a 2013 court-martial of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder and was sentenced to death. He exhausted his regular appeals in 2025. What happened in the Fort Hood shooting? Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center, where soldiers were undergoing medical checkups before deploying, and witnesses testified he shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — before he opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He killed 13 people and wounded more than 30. According to the Associated Press , Hasan said he carried out the shooting to stop soldiers from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He represented himself at his 2013 court-martial and mounted little defense, telling jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides." Why a firing squad rather than lethal injection? The Pentagon did not explain why Hasan would be executed by firing squad rather than lethal injection, the method specified in the military's current execution regulations. It also did not say whether those regulations would need to change. The Army adopted a plan in February for carrying out military executions at the federal government's execution facility in Terre Haute, Ind., ABC News reported in June. Known as Operation Resolute Justice, the plan calls for condemned service members to be transferred there from the military prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., and for the Army to coordinate with the Federal Bureau of Prisons. The Army is to be ready to carry out an execution no sooner than 60 days and within 150 days of presidential approval. ABC's report did not specify an execution method. The Justice Department separately directed the Bureau of Prisons in April to expand its protocol for federal civilian executions to include methods beyond lethal injection, including firing squads. That change does not apply to military executions. Firing squads have also recently returned at the state level. Five states allow them, according to the Death Penalty Information Center : Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho made the firing squad its primary execution method on July 1 after a law signed in 2025 took effect. South Carolina carried out three firing squad executions in 2025, the first uses of the method in the U.S. since 2010. Condemned prisoners there can choose among authorized execution methods. After Pike's failed execution, several top Republicans in Tennessee said they want to explore alternative ways of executing condemned prisoners. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, told the AP , "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully." Top legislative leaders have already spoken with Blackburn about potential changes to state execution laws during their 2027 session. "We want to broaden it, include more methods," Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton said. "What those are as of today, I'm not sure. But I don't think there's any method that's off the table at this point." How common are military executions? Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions are even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kan. President George W. Bush approved the execution of Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008, but a judge put it on hold. Gray remains at Fort Leavenworth. The last person executed under the military justice system was Pvt. John Bennett, who was hanged in 1961 for the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl. item.title: Trump’s daylight saving push runs into a geographic divide in the Senate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The battle over Americans’ clocks reemerged in an unlikely way over the weekend, with President Donald Trump picking a fight with one of his top allies over the issue. There have been many fights in Congress over the nearly two years that Trump has been in office for his second term that either ended in partisan victory or gloriously fizzled out, but one has quietly gone onto the shelf despite his pressure on Republicans to do something about it. And that fight is over allowing states to voluntarily observe daylight saving time year-round to effectively do away with the twice-a-year ritual of changing clocks. It’s a popular issue with voters and the president, and there’s a bill that passed the House this summer to enact the change. But it’s a policy issue that has divided both sides of the aisle and ground to a halt in the upper chamber. Trump Urges Senate To Pass Bill Making Daylight Saving Time Permanent After Overwhelming House Vote President Donald Trump wants to make daylight saving permanent, but a geographic coalition of northern versus southern states are in a heated debate over the merits of the change, which spells doom for the bill. Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., has been one of the more vocal opponents of the bill, vowing to block any attempts to fast-track it on the floor. That resistance earned him a Truth Social post from Trump, who over the weekend shared his personal phone number in a bid to pressure the lawmaker to change his stance on daylight saving time. "Almost everybody wants "The Sunshine Protection Act" to pass, except for Tom Cotton," Trump said. "To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself." Read On The Fox News App Cotton responded, noting that Congress has tackled daylight saving time before, only to roll back the change shortly after. "No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Saving Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton said on X. "Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first." Trump Faces Republican Rebellion Over Daylight Saving Time As Senate Bill Nears Dead End In the 1970s, lawmakers did enact year-round daylight saving time. But Americans rapidly soured on the change, especially parents whose children had to wait in the dark for the school bus. It was repealed about a year later. And Cotton recently answered an off-the-cuff question from a fellow Republican during their weekly closed-door policy lunches, a source told Fox News Digital, where he made a similar case as his response to Trump. No one pushed back during the meeting. The issue of daylight saving time , and supporting a permanent fix or sticking to the status quo are more geographical than political. It’s, in part, mountainous and Western states versus coastal states. On one side of the spectrum are lawmakers like Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and Patty Murray, D-Wash., who introduced a Senate version of the bill last year. "Every year, more Americans grow more frustrated setting their clocks back and forth, and every winter folks in Washington state despair at the prospect of losing an hour of precious sunlight when we are forced off Daylight Saving Time," Murray said in a statement at the time. House Passes Daylight Saving Time Reform As Trump Signals Support For Ending Clock Change Aerial view of downtown Bozeman, Montana at dusk. Lawmakers in landlocked states out West, like Sens. Steve Daines, R-Mont., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., warn that it would cause kids in their states to go to school in the dark. "I can see where Florida likes it for tee times at certain times of the year, but it doesn’t work so well for moms and dads putting kids on buses when the sunrise in Western Montana wouldn’t be till 9:30 in the morning. It’s not going to work for us," Daines told CNN in July. Click Here To Download The Fox News App The most vital currency in the Senate is floor time. And lawmakers won’t have much floor time to spare when they return after the midterm elections in November. Though it’s popular, more pressing issues like the National Defense Authorization Act, supplemental funding for the war and a looming government funding battle will likely take precedence. And Republican leaders acknowledge that it’s not as easy as a simple yes-or-no vote for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. "Depends where you're living in the country and the impact — what it would be, in your own home state," Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said in July. "So it's not as simple as what one state might like." item.title: Cornell taps former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to lead investigation

Thousands of people gathered at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Monday in support of "Jane Doe," the former student who alleges she was drugged and raped by multiple members of a fraternity in October 2024. The "Justice for Survivors" rally was organized by over 20 student organizations who led a late afternoon march to Day Hall, which houses the university's administrative offices and had been vandalized by activists overnight . Students, faculty, and residents from across the state took part in the protest calling for Cornell administrators to resign over their handling of the case. "We are known as the rape school," Saya Taylor, a Cornell sophomore, said at the rally. "We can be known as leading a nationwide reform movement." Demonstrators held signs accusing the Ivy League school of protecting the alleged rapists and demanding accountability. "Jane Doe deserved a campus that supported her," Taylor said. "Jane Doe deserved an administration that delivered a fair and proper judicial process. Jane Doe deserved a police department that would actually follow up on her case. Instead, she was silenced." Late Monday, the Cornell University faculty introduced a resolution declaring it has no confidence in the administration's ability to address the "ongoing crisis of sexual assault" on campus. According to NBC News , the proposal is expected to be considered by the Faculty Senate on Oct. 14. "The goal is to really force systemic change," Faculty Senator Paul Ortiz said in a statement to NBC. "Women need to feel safe." On Monday night, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff and Ryan Lombardi, the school's vice president for student and campus life, met with the Graduate and Professional Student Assembly, which pressed them on their response to Jane Doe's allegations. Cornell students participate in a protest over the university's handling of the "Jane Doe" case on Oct. 5. Spencer Platt via Getty Images "We're all angry. I understand that anger," Kotlikoff said, according to the Cornell Daily Sun . "People want easy answers to this." He added: "This passion, if appropriately channeled, can help us as a community address this issue." On Tuesday, Cornell's board of trustees announced it has retained former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, a partner at law firm King & Spalding, to lead an independent review of how the university responds to sexual assault on campus. "As part of that broader mandate, Yates and her team will conduct a detailed review of the University's response to the allegations involving Jane Doe and members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, including whether Cornell followed its policies and procedures in responding to the matter," the board of trustees said in a statement . The developments came hours after audio of a phone call between Jane Doe and one of the accused fraternity members, recorded weeks after the alleged incident, was released by ABC News . During the call, Jane Doe said she was "10 shots deep" when she arrived at the Chi Phi fraternity house and was now struggling to remember what had caused "so much damage on my body and brain." "The only way for me to heal is to know what happened," she said. "That's why I'm trying to just piece it together, you know, like I'm just like confused." The fraternity member told her that she consented to having a threesome with him and another fraternity brother. He also insisted that Jane Doe had told him she had not been drinking when she showed up. "You did tell me you were sober, by the way," he said. "You said you hadn't been anywhere." "That is not true. I never would have said that," she replied. The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Oct. 1. Matt Rourke/AP At one point during the Nov. 7, 2024, call, Jane Doe told him, "If I wanted to take this somewhere, what y'all did would be classified as gang rape." The fraternity member then suggested that their memory of what transpired may be inaccurate. "I have racked my brain for this mystery," he said. "You know, it's possible that both of us, like, remember this, and it's not true." Jane Doe pushed back: "No, because I remember looking up and being like, 'That is too many people.'" Read more from Yahoo: A timeline of the Cornell University rape case ABC News also reported this week that a day after a campus-wide alert notified students of the reported rape at Chi Phi, Cornell's police department received an anonymous tip from a caller who said that the fraternity's leadership asked a potential witness to stay quiet because "the reputation of all involved and the frat would be ruined" if details were made public. According to the report, one female student also told Cornell investigators that the fraternity "held a meeting essentially to get all of the men on the same page about what happened." The fraternity members described the incident as a "consensual orgy," but expressed concern that it "would be bad for our image," the same student told investigators. A student wears a Jane Doe name tag during a rally at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Oct. 5. REUTERS / REUTERS Other calls and text messages obtained by ABC News suggested that some of the fraternity members attempted to contain the allegations in the weeks that followed. "When was the last time you spoke to [Jane Doe]?" the fraternity's president wrote in the messages to the member who invited Jane Doe to the house. "Yesterday ... what's the plan of action?" he replied. "Should I call [Jane Doe]? I don't think she would have reported this." Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the alleged 2024 rape, reported the incident to Cornell University police on Nov. 8, 2024. She filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16 against the school, seven current and former Chi Phi fraternity members, the Tri-Delta Alpha Beta sorority where she lived, and a local bar where she said she was served alcohol on the night of the alleged incident. All of the men identified in Jane Doe's civil suit have denied any wrongdoing, according to the New York Times . None has been charged with a crime. And Chi Phi remains banned from campus. Students participate in the march and protest at Cornell University on Oct. 5. Spencer Platt via Getty Images In court papers filed on Monday, the owners of Moonies Bar and Nightclub denied that they "sold, furnished or assisted in procuring alcoholic beverages to any person under [the] legal drinking age" or "any visibly intoxicated person." They also said they "neither knew nor should have known any assault would occur," and had no obligation to protect Jane Doe from "sudden criminal acts of third parties off premises." Cornell University has come under intense scrutiny for its handling of the case. In an eight-minute video statement released on Saturday, Kotlikoff, Cornell's president, said the university "must do better." "What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come. My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," Kotlikoff said. "It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use. It also raises questions around the investigations conducted after the allegations were reported." People participate in a "Justice For Survivors" rally at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Oct. 5. Spencer Platt via Getty Images New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said on Friday that the woman was "failed" by those obligated to protect her, including university police and a prosecutor who initially declined to bring charges. Hochul said that she had lost faith in Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten and appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as the special prosecutor to oversee the criminal investigation. "This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable," the governor said. "And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her." "There are people out there trying to track her down," Giuffra said on CNN's State of the Union on Sunday. "They said we're gonna shut you up. You're gonna still get hurt by us. You're gonna pull this lawsuit out or we're gonna do something to hurt you even more." item.title: Gatorade recalls 122,000 cases over undeclared food dyes. Check these flavors.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
More than 122,000 cases of Gatorade have been voluntarily recalled because they may contain undeclared food dyes, according to a Food and Drug Administration alert . The recall affects 28-ounce bottles of four flavors of yellow and orange Gatorade sold in 37 states. They may be colored with synthetic food dyes, Yellow No. 6 and Yellow No. 5, or both, but the labels of the recalled products didn't properly disclose those ingredients. While both dyes are legal for companies to use in food and beverage products, they have to be declared on labels because, in rare cases, they can cause allergic reactions , including hives, wheezing and asthma attacks. The recall comes after PepsiCo — which makes Gatorade — announced in April 2025 that it would transition away from synthetic dyes in favor of natural ones. It's part of the company's efforts to comply with U.S. health officials' encouragement for food and beverage companies to stop using artificial coloring. What products are affected? PepsiCo has issued a voluntary recall of cases of Gatorade Lemon Lime, Gatorade Lemon Lime Zero, Gatorade Orange and Gatorade Orange Zero. The products were shipped to more than three dozen states, including Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, North Dakota, New York and Texas. The recall was initiated on Sept. 25, but — to the frustration of two experts who spoke with Yahoo — wasn't published by the FDA until Oct. 2, when the agency said it was a Class II recall (meaning the products could cause temporary health problems, but the risk of serious health issues is "remote"). Both experts Yahoo spoke with said that, if you or someone in your household has a food dye allergy and recently purchased any of these Gatorade products, you should check the labels against the lot numbers listed in the FDA alert . What are the risks? Because so many bottles of Gatorade were recalled, "the scale is certainly significant," Thomas Gremillion , director of food policy at the Consumer Federation of America, told Yahoo. The good news is that allergies to food additives in general, and food dyes in particular, are exceedingly rare . Still, these dyes have to be disclosed because they can cause severe reactions, including, in at least a few cases, anaphylaxis. "The kind of issues this can cause — hives, breathing issues, swelling of the throat or tongue — this could be quite serious," Teresa Murray , consumer watchdog director at the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), told Yahoo. To prevent these reactions, companies are required to declare potential allergens on their product packaging. The labels for bottles of Lemon Lime Gatorade , for example, do typically list "Yellow 5" as one of the ingredients. A spokesperson for PepsiCo told Yahoo that the recall was due to a labeling issue, not to the ingredients in the products themselves. "These food dyes are permitted, [companies] just have to disclose them — so just do it!" Murray said. No health problems related to the recalled bottles of Gatorade have been reported. And, Murray adds that "because it's reasonable to assume that the yellow and orange Gatorades have included this dye for a long time, it's also reasonable to think that you don't have people buying this that are allergic to it." Is this related to the new bans on food dyes? In 2025, the FDA banned Red Dye No. 3 and has since revoked authorization for a rarely used orange dye . The agency has also proposed banning another outdated additive, Citrus Red No. 2 , and is working with food and beverage manufacturers to phase out all artificial food dyes . Synthetic food dyes are made from petroleum, and some studies have linked Red Dye No. 3 to increased cancer risk in rats. Other research suggests that kids — especially those with ADHD — who consume a lot of artificial food coloring, including Yellow No. 5 and Yellow No. 6, may be at greater risk for behavioral issues. Concerns over cancer and attention disorders are among U.S. health officials' motivations for urging companies to stop using artificial dyes. Yellow colorings are not currently banned, so the recall is not directly related to the new restrictions or calls for companies to voluntarily eliminate the dyes from their products. PepsiCo is in the midst of voluntarily swapping petroleum-based dyes for natural coloring, and introduced artificial flavor- and color-free versions of its Doritos and Cheetos in December. But it's unclear where Gatorade products are in the transition process. "It's certainly intriguing that they've said they're going to phase out these artificial dyes," and now there's a recall related to one, says Gremillion. item.title: Justice Samuel Alito says same-sex marriage ruling marked a turn against religious liberty
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito , the devout Catholic conservative who has long warned of animus against religion in America, says in a new book that he believes the court's landmark decision extending marriage rights to same-sex couples was "perhaps the decisive point in our nation's turn against religious liberty." Alito, who dissented sharply in the 2015 case, made the claim at Catholic University of America three years after Obergefell v Hodges in a speech that was not open to the public or widely covered at the time. The remarks were published this month in "So Ordered," a collection of Alito speeches that he says reflect his judicial philosophy and outlook on the country. J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo - PHOTO: Associate Justice Samuel Alito stands in his chambers at the Supreme Court during an Associated Press interview, in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026. Seven of the 19 Alito speeches published in the book were delivered to Catholic groups. "In dissent from that ruling," he said in the 2018 address, "I expressed my worry that equating the expression of certain views with bigotry -- or, if you like, with dignitary harm -- would drive believers out of public life." Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images, FILE - PHOTO: In this Feb. 23, 2016, file photo, Supreme Court Associate Justice Samuel Alito speaks in Washington, D.C. Alito suggests that his prediction has come to pass. "Quite suddenly, religious liberty has become controversial," Alito said in a newly published 2022 speech to the Magnificat Foundation, a nonprofit group dedicated to promoting Catholic culture and traditions. Supreme Court temporarily extends access to abortion pill mifepristone by mail Throughout the book, the justice cites a string of lawsuits to reach the Supreme Court in recent years as evidence that, in his opinion, "support for religious liberty has cratered." The cases he uses as examples involve businesses threatened with punishment for refusing to provide services for gay weddings and faith-based organizations harmed by government health or employment regulations without any religious exemption. "What we see in these and other cases," Alito says in the 2022 speech, "is a refusal to live in peace with those who violate the new moral code." He says the dynamic will "virtually guarantee that the Supreme Court will continue to see a steady stream of religious-liberty cases." Court sided with religiously affiliated parties In nearly all the cases Alito cites as examples of religious animus, the court ultimately sided with the religiously affiliated parties over their opponents. The court ruled in favor of a Colorado baker who was sued for refusing to create a wedding cake for a gay couple and later defended a Christian wedding website designer who objected to creating sites for same-sex ceremonies. Alex Wong/Getty Images, FILE - PHOTO: In this June 26, 2015, file photo, same-sex marriage supporters rejoice after the U.S Supreme Court hands down a ruling regarding same-sex marriage outside the Supreme Court in Washington, D.C. When the Affordable Care Act mandated that employers provide insurance plans with no-cost contraceptive coverage, the high court ruled that some private employers can opt-out as a matter of faith and that federal agencies must be allowed to exempt religious employers from the rule. The court recently ruled that states must allow religiously affiliated private schools to participate in state-funded private tuition programs and tax credit initiatives . Last year, it gave parents the right to opt-out their kids from teachings that conflict with sincere religious beliefs. The conservative majority blocked a bid by the city of Philadelphia to exclude Catholic Social Services from its foster care program over LGBT discrimination and later effectively struck down state laws banning LGBT conversion therapy, which some religious advocates said amounted to a gag order against Christian teaching about human sexuality. Supreme Court Justices Alito, Thomas not expected to retire this year: Sources Recent decisions have also expanded protection for religious exercise on the job -- siding with a former public school football coach who had been disciplined for praying at midfield after games -- and mandated broader employer accommodations for the faithful who need to skip work to attend worship services. Sandy Huffaker/AFP via Getty Images, FILE - PHOTO: In this June 20, 2025, file photo, worshipers attend a special Mass at the Cathedral of St. Joseph in San Diego, Calif. Alito joined the majority in all of those cases and has voted in favor of faith-based interests in many others over his 20 years on the high court. Same-sex marriage remains a flashpoint The issue of same-sex marriage rights, which was narrowly decided 5-4, remains a flashpoint. Many LGBTQ advocates have begun to fear, in part from public criticism aired by Justice Alito, that Obergefell may not be on settled ground. In 2025, Alito said publicly that while he strongly opposes the ruling, he is "not suggesting that the decision should be overruled," even as fellow conservative Justice Clarence Thomas has openly urged his colleagues to do so. Nevertheless, Alito suggests in his book that the marriage decision has effectively silenced Americans whose sincere religious beliefs favor limiting unions to one man and one woman, likening them to Catholics who were sidelined in post-Reformation England. They "had been so beaten down that they were 'a people who shunned the light of day.' They were 'found in corners, and alleys, and cellars, and the housetops, or in the recesses of the country,'" he said in a newly-published speech delivered in 2021 at Thomas Aquinas College. "What I predicted in my dissent is coming to pass," Alito said of same-sex marriage opponents. Some advocates see differently than Alito While many religious liberty advocates openly share Alito's concerns, some have voiced a different view of the current state of affairs. Andrew Medichini/AP Photo, FILE - PHOTO: In this Sept. 20, 2025, file photo, Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito attends a meeting in Rome. item.title: Fake Jane Does are flooding the internet to protect the plaintiff in Cornell rape case
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Supporters have launched an online campaign in recent weeks aimed at protecting the identity of a woman, identified as " Jane Doe , " who alleges in a civil lawsuit that she was drugged and raped by multiple members of a Cornell University fraternity in 2024. Jane Doe's lawyer says that the ex-Cornell student has received " multiple threats " in recent days aimed at exposing her real identity. "There are people out there trying to track her down," Thomas Giuffra, who ‌represents Jane Doe, told CNN's State of the Union on Sunday. "They said, 'We're gonna shut you up. You're gonna still get hurt by us. You're gonna pull this lawsuit out or we're gonna do something to hurt you even more.' "The threats, the abuse to protect what's going on, the status quo — these guys are disgusting," Giuffra added. Among those trying to identify Jane Doe is political commentator Michael Tracey, who publicly asked anyone with information about her identity to contact him and said he would publish her name and identifying details. The possibility that Jane Doe's true identity might be revealed mobilized many social media users to post "I am Jane Doe" in an effort to protect the identity of the former Cornell University student. Hundreds of Cornell students participated in a rally about the rape case on Oct. 5 in Ithaca. Spencer Platt/Getty Images The goal of the movement is to show solidarity with Jane Doe and to make online searches for the woman's identity less useful by returning a mix of conflicting "Jane Doe" identities. Some TikTok users have been sharing their own experiences with sexual assault and overlaying "I am Jane Doe" text over the video. In a Reddit thread , some users are taking it a step further by deliberately using false identities, including fictional characters or celebrities. "Jane Doe's name? Nunya. Nunya Business," one user commented. "Of course I know the identity of Jane Doe, the plaintiff against Cornell and the Cornell 7. Jane Doe is Robert California," another user wrote, referring to the fictional character from The Office . According to Chirag Shah, a professor at the University of Washington's Information School, the tactic has a name. "Typically, this is a form of information poisoning," Shah told Yahoo. "People do it for different intents to confuse people, to slow them down or to divert them to other things." Shah said this strategy is commonly associated with misinformation campaigns, online scams and efforts to manipulate search results. He said this recent strategy stands out because many participants appear to be motivated to protect the plaintiff's identity. "If the intent here is to protect Jane Doe, which, on the social side of it, is very admirable, on the technical side of it, it's not really possible," Shah said. "But what it ends up doing is creating friction." He explained that while the friction might discourage casual internet sleuths, it's unlikely to conceal someone's identity from those determined to uncover it. "Most people don't have the time, motivation or skills to really investigate," Shah said. "But somebody who really wants to do this, they can cut through this noise." An attendee wears a name tag reading "Jane Doe" during an Oct. 5 protest in Ithaca. Adrian Kraus/AP The online movement has sparked discussion about whether flooding the internet with false identities could confuse search engines and AI chatbots. Shah said modern systems are designed to combat attempts by bad actors to spread false information. "Because this is not a new phenomenon, the existing search engines, including the chatbots, are designed to counteract a lot of these things," Shah said. "Even if it works, it would only work temporarily." Search engines also increasingly weigh the credibility and reliability of sources rather than simply counting mentions of a claim, he explained. A surge of coordinated posts might temporarily influence results, but Shah said those systems are built to recognize unusual spikes and eventually correct for them. Volume can still matter in specific ways, he added. If "I am Jane Doe" posts are associated with one celebrity's name, it will generate more volume and receive more attention, but it could easily be discredited if the celebrity clearly is not the former Cornell student. "If the intent is to leave people confused, you're better off giving all kinds of [names]," Shah said, comparing it to the "Two Truths and a Lie" game. "If you tell a million lies and one is true, it's much harder to find, and people then just give up. "So that strategy often works." Shah said the campaign itself is fascinating to him because it flips a tactic usually used by bad actors into one being used by people who believe they are protecting someone vulnerable. "All these times I have talked about misinformation and disinformation campaigns, this is the first time it's sort of on this side," Shah said. "If I were ever to look for a good case of a misinformation campaign," he added, "this would be it." item.title: Olympian accused of damaging Reflecting Pool seeks probe of potential misconduct
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Attorneys for Olympic canoeist David Hearn asked the internal watchdogs at the Justice and Interior departments on Tuesday to investigate the circumstances surrounding his arrest, indictment and the dismissal of the case, according to a letter seen by CBS News. Hearn's case garnered national attention, after he was falsely accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and subsequently indicted on a charge of felony destruction of government property. Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, later moved to dismiss the case after she said new information had come to light showing the damage had been caused by a contractor's "botched installation," not vandalism. "Because of the actions of various DOJ and DOI employees, Mr. Hearn was deprived of his liberty, indicted for a crime he did not commit, threatened with incarceration of up to 10 years, and endured the defaming of his name and reputation by high-ranking government officials," Hearn's attorneys wrote in the letter to DOJ Inspector General Don Berthiaume and DOI Inspector General Caryl Brzymialkiewicz. Those officials, they pointed out, included Pirro, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and President Trump. "The DOJ OIG and the DOI OIG must conduct detailed and comprehensive investigations to determine what happened inside their agencies that led to the shocking and indefensible treatment of Mr. Hearn," they wrote. "Anything less than a full and fair review would be a betrayal of your mission and perpetuate the outrageous mistreatment of Mr. Hearn." Hearn was initially detained in jail for five hours on June 19, after he stopped by the Reflecting Pool during a bike ride. He put his hand into the water and touched a piece of the liner that had already come loose before he was asked by a member of the National Park Police to remove his hand from the water. His lawyers said that during his five-hour detention, he was never read his Miranda rights or permitted to make a phone call, and that he only learned he was initially facing misdemeanor charges when he found two citations stuffed into a brown paper bag with his other belongings shortly after his release from custody. A grand jury in the D.C. Superior Court later indicted him on the felony count on July 2. Despite a request from Hearn's attorneys to preserve the physical evidence in the case, his lawyers said the government fenced off the area around the Reflecting Pool in question and undertook repairs to the section of the liner that was at the heart of the indictment. By the end of July, Pirro moved to dismiss the case altogether, alleging that the Interior Department had delayed producing materials to prosecutors that undermined the evidentiary basis for the case. "The record reflects an indictment obtained through unusual haste and a prosecution shaped from the outset by political pressure and built on an inadequate investigation," Hearn's lawyers wrote in the letter to the inspectors general. Pirro was later spotted toting a large box into the White House that sources later confirmed to CBS News contained evidence from the case that she presented to Mr. Trump, after he lashed out at her for dismissing the case against Hearn. The White House has since held meetings with prosecutors to explore whether other charges could be brought. But a Superior Court Judge foreclosed that possibility on Oct. 1, after he ruled that the case had to be dismissed with prejudice — meaning it cannot be brought again. "Should the Court dismiss this case in a fashion that allows the government to reinitiate prosecution in the future, the Court would be exposing him to the risk that, due to pressure from the President Of the United States apparently motivated at least in part by Mr. Hearn's political views, he would again be charged with a crime that prosecutors have determined he did not commit," the judge wrote in the opinion dismissing the case. The letter alleges that prosecutors had exculpatory evidence in hand before they sought an indictment against Hearn. It also alleges that Pirro improperly approached one of the defense's expert witnesses who was inspecting the Reflecting Pool and peppered the expert with questions. "Defense counsel was given no notice that the encounter would take place and was not present for it, and the government has never produced any report, note, or record of the exchange," Hearn's attorneys wrote. They continued, "A U.S. Attorney who personally interrogates a represented defendant's testifying expert, in the field, surrounded by her own staff and without notice to counsel, is not gathering evidence—she is testing how the defense intends to prove its case." They also accused Pirro of running afoul of the rules of professional conduct for attorneys when she spoke publicly about the case during a press conference, and questioned whether the sole grand jury witness in the case had been recalled in order to "manufacture" a damages estimate to help support the felony charge. Hearn's lawyers also complained that Pirro's statements announcing the indictment "extended well beyond the bare fact of the charge." "[S]he previewed anticipated witness testimony, vouched for the credibility of government witnesses, opined directly on Mr. Hearn's guilt, and characterized the alleged conduct as 'anarchy' and 'criminal behavior' — conduct implicating the trial-publicity and prosecutorial-conduct constraints of D.C. Rules of Professional Conduct," Hearn's attorneys wrote. A Justice Department spokesperson said, "The Office of the Inspector General operates independently and makes its own decisions about what to review." item.title: Trump allows tax-free red diesel on U.S. highways as fuel prices soar for truckers
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday evening temporarily allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on public roads and deferring the federal excise tax on that fuel through the end of the year, a move aimed at lowering costs for truckers and farmers facing record-high diesel prices. Red-dyed diesel is chemically the same product as standard highway diesel, but carries a red dye to mark it as off-road fuel — meaning it is not subject to the 24.4-cent-per-gallon federal excise tax that applies to diesel sold at the pump for road use, such as for tractors and heavy machinery. Using it in highway vehicles has been illegal, carrying penalties for tax evasion, according to CNBC . According to the White House, the order instructs the Treasury Secretary to hold off on collecting federal excise taxes on highway use of dyed diesel between October 5 and December 31, 2026, and to do so without charging interest or imposing penalties. The Treasury is also directed to direct the Internal Revenue Service not to impose penalties for on-road use of dyed diesel during that period. The order further instructs officials to explore pathways, including legislation, to eliminate the deferred tax obligations entirely. The White House projected that a trucker who tops off an 18-wheeler's tank with 250 gallons stands to save over $100 on a single fill-up, provided the trucker's state suspends its own diesel tax as well. On top of the federal levy, each state levies its own diesel excise tax, and those state-level taxes average out to 35.5 cents per gallon, according to CNN . The order also directs the Secretary of Agriculture to coordinate with agricultural cooperatives and rural fuel distributors to ensure adequate dyed diesel distribution in high-demand areas, and the Secretary of Transportation to engage with state governments and industry stakeholders. The White House Office of Intergovernmental Affairs was directed to encourage states to adopt corresponding policies. Diesel prices surged from $3.76 a gallon before the Iran war to a record national average of $6.53 a gallon on September 22, according to AAA data. As of Tuesday, the national average stood at $6.32 a gallon. Behind the price surge are several converging pressures: supply dislocations tied to the Iran conflict, Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian oil refineries — which led the Kremlin to curtail diesel exports — and a worldwide deficit in refining output. Trump announced the order at a rally in Nebraska on Monday evening. "We're not going to need it long, I hope, we're not going to need it long because your prices are plummeting and they're going to really be plummeting," Trump said, according to CNN. Several states had already moved in this direction before the federal order. In the roughly ten days before the federal order, a total of ten states — among them Texas, Oklahoma, North Carolina, and Alabama — had already moved to open up access to dyed diesel for drivers on public roads, according to CNN, which cited a count from research firm ClearView Energy Partners. The diesel crisis had drawn pressure on the administration from Capitol Hill. Earlier, as Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley called for an embargo on U.S. diesel exports , arguing that record fuel prices were devastating farmers and truckers, Trump instead pursued the international route: last week, the Group of Seven nations agreed to release up to 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks following sustained U.S. pressure on European allies.
